tagline.text: A fortress church and lighthouse island at the mouth of San Bernardino Strait

location.label: Location
location.text: Capul municipality, Northern Samar (Capul Island, 12 barangays)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: December–May, when the sea is relatively calm

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,500–3,500 (per person, 1 night 2 days, including transport, lodging and meals from Tacloban)

children.text: Capul is a small island municipality at the southern entrance of San Bernardino Strait, home to the Church of St. Ignatius of Loyola, walled in against pirate raids, and a lighthouse built in 1896. The Abaknon language spoken by residents is the only distinct language in Northern Samar, which makes the island interesting as a cultural destination too.

Capul is an island municipality in Northern Samar, where one island makes up one town. It sits at the southern entrance of San Bernardino Strait, which separates Luzon and Samar, and was a waypoint for the galleons that sailed between Manila and Acapulco, Mexico. The area is about

and the highest point is 585 m above sea level. It has 12 barangays (Aguin, Jubang, Landusan, Oson, Poblacion 1–5, Sagaosawan, San Luis and Sawang). The 2024 census counted 12,127 residents in about 2,700 households.

What makes Capul special for travelers is its history and its language. According to oral tradition, the ancestors of the Abaknon people came from Balabac Island south of Palawan and belong to the Sama-Bajau family. Around the 14th century, when Balabac was annexed by the Sultanate of Sulu, those who refused to convert to Islam are said to have fled under a datu named Abak and settled here. As a result, the local language Inabaknon is classified as a Sama-Bajaw language and is said to be unintelligible to speakers of Waray or Cebuano. It is the only town in Northern Samar with a language of its own. Most residents also understand Waray and Tagalog, so travel is not a problem.

Spanish Jesuit missionaries arrived on the island around 1610, and the first church was built around then. The Church of St. Ignatius of Loyola that stands today is the third church on the same site. The first two were destroyed in Moro pirate raids in 1615 and 1768, and in 1781 Fr. Mariano Valero led the restoration and is said to have surrounded it with a stone fortress resembling Intramuros in Manila. Capul also served as the capital of Samar Province from 1848 to 1852. The story that the island's name comes from Acapulco is likewise tied to the galleon trade.

Capul is not a tourist resort with hotels and tour buses but a remote island with limited boats and electricity. In return, coastal rock formations, white sand beaches, an old church and fortress, wartime tunnels and a lighthouse that few visitors reach are all gathered on one island. Sea weather can upset your plans, so leave a spare day, and since transport and fares change from year to year, please check the latest information before you go.

blocks.title: Church of St. Ignatius of Loyola and the fortress

children.text: This Spanish colonial church in the Poblacion has thick coral-stone walls designed to withstand Moro pirate raids. A square fortress surrounds the church, with bulwarks of different designs at the corners of the wall. A small exhibit space inside is also reported. Sources give the construction date as either the 1600s or the 18th century, which fits the fact that the church was rebuilt several times on the same site. Please be quiet during Mass times.

This stone watchtower stands on a hill near the fortress. It was a warning post that looked down on the town harbor for approaching pirates, and a refuge for residents during raids. Today it makes a good lookout over the harbor and the sea.

This Spanish-era lighthouse stands at Totoog Point in San Luis and is said to have been built in 1896. It is still in operation and guides ships through San Bernardino Strait. On the hill below it are a rock formation called Big Foot and a natural saltwater pool. It is also considered a good place to watch sunrise and sunset.

Near the southern tip of the island is a rudder-shaped rock formation, and the beach around it has fine sand and clear water. With almost no development, it suits swimming, picnics and sunsets. Do not go near the rocks when the waves are rough.

This sea cave in Sawang has small pools along the rocky shore, and some people go cliff diving there. Access to the cave changes with the tide and the floor can be slippery, so go with a local guide and bring a headlamp.

Abak Beach in Oson is the beach where a resort stands, and Oot Beach is described as having clear water good for snorkeling. Few places rent equipment, so it is safer to bring your own mask and snorkel. There is coral, so do not stand on it or touch it.

The residential areas still have houses built on stilts and old wood-and-nipa homes. Residents are generally friendly and love to chat, and learning a few Abaknon greetings will be appreciated. Ask permission before photographing people or private property.

The island is said to have three foxholes (bomb-shelter trenches) that residents used as air-raid shelters during World War II, along with old war tunnels. Moro-Moro Point has good coastal views. Ask a local guide for exact locations.
Take a van from Tacloban to Allen, go to the port, and board a boat that leaves before noon. The boat ride takes about
45 minutes to 1 hour
Get off at Capul port and drop your bags at your lodging. There are almost no restaurants, so ask your lodging to prepare lunch.
Walk around the Church of St. Ignatius of Loyola, the fortress and the watchtower, then look at the village houses.
Watch the sunset from Timon-Timon beach or the coastal rocks. Electricity on the island is limited, so use a flashlight.
Visit the lighthouse at Totoog Point around sunrise and see the Big Foot rock and the natural pool.
Return to the port in time for an afternoon boat and head back to Allen.
Boat schedules change often and depend on the weather. Ask your lodging or the boatman the day before so you do not miss the boat on your return day.

items.title: Via Victoria and San Antonio Island

children.text: This route takes a boat from Victoria, the town next to Allen, to San Antonio Island (Dalupiri), then a motorcycle taxi to Sitio Dalupirit, where you charter a boat to Capul.

You can also explore the coconut-lined roads and coastal villages by bike or on foot.
Capul gets about 1,352 mm of rain a year, with rain on around 250 days. The driest month is March (about 58 mm) and the wettest is October (about 165 mm). Average daily highs range from about
in January to about
in May.

Boat service across the strait is the biggest variable on this island. It is safest to go in December–May, when the sea is relatively calm, and in typhoon season boats can stop and leave you stranded on the island.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: The northeast monsoon can make the sea rough, so check boats.
The calmest sea of the year. Good for beaches and snorkeling.
Typhoons and rough seas often cancel boats, so leave slack in your schedule.

There are no luxury hotels, only simple lodging. Known places include Abak Beach Resort in Oson (phone +63 920 439 1061), Acapulco Island Beach Resort in San Luis, Alisampan Beach Resort, Korongkorong Beach Resort and private homestays. In the 2013 guide a homestay cost about
per night, which may have changed, and some travelers camp on the beach or near the lighthouse. Confirm contact details and rates in advance.

Food centers on fresh seafood, coconut milk and home cooking with local ingredients. Restaurants are few, so ask your lodging to prepare meals in advance or bring snacks. The island has no ATM and nowhere accepts cards, and one guide says electricity is only on in the evening (about
); a 2023 guide says power is on 24 hours, so accounts differ. Bring a power bank.
Bring plenty of cash. The island has no ATM and cards cannot be used.
Electricity may be limited, so bring a power bank and a flashlight.
Globe and Smart get a signal in some places but it is weak in others. Make important calls in Allen beforehand.
Boats are canceled in bad weather, so leave slack on your return day.
Snorkeling gear is hard to rent, so bring your own mask and snorkel.
The sun is strong, so bring a hat, sunglasses and sunscreen, and carry plenty of drinking water.
Respect Abaknon culture, and ask permission before photographing people or private property.
Carry your trash back out. Waste disposal facilities on the island are limited.
The waters off Capul are San Bernardino Strait, with strong currents and frequent rough seas. Boats can be suspended suddenly because of weather, so always confirm your return boat.
When boarding a bangka, ask for a life jacket and avoid boats that exceed their capacity.
Coastal rocks and caves are dangerous with the tide and waves. Do not enter without a local guide.
The church, fortress and lighthouse are part of local people's daily and religious life. Be quiet during Mass.
Emergency medical facilities are limited, so bring your own basic medicines.
